headline: Keep production: no candidate passes more requests without losing ground, since {arm:v2} fails far more billing requests and {arm:v4} stops citing policy on tone replies.
lede: Both losses are clear of zero after correcting for every comparison the campaign made, and {arm:v3} separates from production on nothing at the same price. What could change the answer is a {arm:v4} that cites policy again: it costs {cost.uplift.v4|abs|pct} less per reply, but on {aspects.billing.cases|words} cases its billing and tone readings are unresolved.
flag: Each request set ran {aspects.billing.cases|words} cases: only large differences separate from production, so most candidate readings here are unresolved, not equal.

decision.text: Keep production. The question allowed a switch only for a candidate that passes more requests without losing any set, and none does.

{arm:v2}: the only candidate clearly better anywhere, on the tone set, but down {aspects.billing.contrast.v2.passed.delta|abs|pts} points on billing. {arm:v4}: {cost.uplift.v4|abs|pct} cheaper per reply, but its policy-citation drop on tone replies breaks the floor set for it. {arm:v3}: separates from production on no set and costs the same, so switching buys nothing.

{arm:v4} is the option that could reverse this. Even with its citations fixed, its billing drop could reach {aspects.billing.flip_margin.v4|abs|pts} points against a margin of {aspects.billing.margin|int}, so today's run cannot clear it. Code's dominance reading names {arm:v2} as dominating production because it counts the tone gain and treats no floor as a gate; {arm:v2}'s billing floor is broken on its whole interval, which the question's own rule forbids. No check grades tone itself: the tone set is scored on totals and policy citation, so {arm:v2}'s tone gain is a gain in getting totals right on those requests.
Fix {arm:v4}'s policy citations on tone requests, then re-run it on billing and tone with more cases: the only route this campaign leaves to a cheaper model.

method.text: {aspects.billing.cases|words} cases per request set, one run per case, except {arm:v3} on the tone set, which ran each case {aspects.tone.depth.v3.repeats|words} times.

Each reply gets two scripted checks: its total matches the case's total, and it cites policy. The campaign does not state its pass rule; on every set the pass counts match the replies that pass both. No judge and no human rating are involved.

Changes against production are contrasts corrected together by Holm's method across {aspects.billing.family.family_size|words} comparisons, each interval at {aspects.billing.family.level}. Rates by arm carry confidence intervals over cases.

Whether a candidate stays within a margin, and the margin at which that flips, are read on each arm's own reading interval; the charts show the corrected contrasts, whose intervals are wider. Both read the same direction for every arm and set.

Each set allows a candidate to fall {aspects.billing.margin|int} points behind production. The tone set's floor speaks for policy citation, not for the tone pass rate, and allows {aspects.tone.floor.tone/rate_drop/reply.cites_policy.v4.margin|int} points; the two are shown apart.
A fixed cost per reply for each arm, the same on every case.
Latency was not recorded. No traffic shares were declared, so no routing between arms was weighed.
The evidence frozen for campaign s1 on its run date, {meta.run_date}.
